What a PRD Becomes When the Reader Can Build

The useful question is not "how short should a PRD be now?" It is "what is the expected cost of the sentence I am about to delete?" — and that quantity has a formula, three inputs, and a startlingly wide range across product types. Teams that thin their specifications without computing it are not being modern. They are placing an uncosted bet on their own review capacity.

1. Two rooms, thirteen days apart

On 6 March 2026, Rohan Sethi had a slide he did not believe. Rohan was vice-president of product at Utsarg Mobility, a Bengaluru company that ran a battery-swap and charging network for electric two- and three-wheelers across nine cities, with a consumer app that about 14 lakh riders used each month to find a swap station, reserve a slot and pay. Utsarg sat in a crowded, real market — Ather's and Ola's own charging networks, Sun Mobility's swap stations, Jio-BP's forecourts — and it competed on one thing: the rider's confidence that a working battery would be there when they arrived.

The slide said that Squad Tarai, which had adopted a prototype-first practice in October, had shipped 2.6 times as many changes per engineer-week as the rest of the organisation. The squad's product manager had stopped writing PRDs altogether. He wrote a paragraph, generated a working candidate with an AI coding assistant, and let the team react to the thing itself. The CEO wanted the practice generalised across all six squads by the start of the new financial year. Rohan's difficulty was that he had also pulled the lead-time numbers, and between October and February the median time from "candidate ready" to "merged and released" in Squad Tarai had gone from 1.6 days to 9.4 days. Throughput measured at the wrong point in the pipeline had risen. Throughput measured at the customer had risen by 31 per cent, not 160.

Thirteen days later, on 19 March, Devika Kulkarni faced the opposite pressure in Pune. Devika was head of product at Nirupan Health Systems, which sold revenue-cycle software to about 210 hospitals — the system that assembles a cashless pre-authorisation packet, submits it to an insurer or third-party administrator under the IRDAI's cashless framework, tracks the query-and-response cycle, and reconciles the settlement. Nirupan did ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue. Its engineering was in Pune and Bengaluru, its design lead in Berlin, its data science lead in Toronto, and its largest customer relationship was managed from Singapore.

Nirupan's chief technology officer had returned from a conference with a target: cut specification effort by 70 per cent. Devika's objection was not sentimental. Nirupan's hospitals were audited. When an insurer disputed a packet, Nirupan had to be able to show which requirement produced a field, when it was introduced, who approved it, and which test demonstrated it. Under the DPDP Act, it had to show what personal data each feature touched and why. A specification at Nirupan was not only an instruction to build; it was a legal artefact and an audit trail. And yet Devika knew, because she had run the same experiment Rohan had, that roughly half of what her team wrote was being reproduced by the assistant without being told.

Two companies, two directions of travel, one underlying question: once the reader can build, which sentences are still worth writing, and how would you know?

2. The idea, its history, and the camps

Define the object precisely. A product requirements document is a written artefact that performs five distinguishable functions, which historically travelled together because they were cheap to staple into one file. It transmits intent — the problem, the user, the outcome, the metric. It transmits build instruction — behaviour specified in enough detail that an implementer need not guess. It performs coordination — telling support, legal, finance and sales what is coming. It creates a record — the reason a rule exists, for the person who inherits it. And it fixes acceptance — the basis on which work is declared correct.

The intellectual history matters because each camp in today's argument is a revival of an older position. Winston Royce's 1970 paper, usually misread as an endorsement of waterfall, was in fact an argument that documentation is what makes a large project reviewable by anyone other than its author. David Parnas gave the field its sharpest formulation in 1986 with "A Rational Design Process: How and Why to Fake It" — the design process is never rational, but the document should be written as though it were, because the document's audience is the future maintainer, not the past author. Fred Brooks, in 1975, argued that the scarce good is conceptual integrity and that a written specification is how one mind's coherence reaches many hands. Donald Gause and Gerald Weinberg's Exploring Requirements (1989) treated ambiguity as the central failure and gave us the discipline of deliberately generating alternative readings. IEEE 830 turned all of it into a checklist that most teams eventually abandoned.

Against that tradition stands Peter Naur's 1985 essay "Programming as Theory Building", which is the most important piece of writing for the present argument and the least read. Naur held that the real asset of a software team is not the code or the document but the theory — the shared mental model of why the system is shaped as it is — held in the heads of the people who built it. Documents are a lossy projection of the theory. A team that loses the theory cannot modify its own product intelligently, even with perfect documentation. The relevance is immediate: if writing the specification was how the theory got built, then deleting the writing may destroy the theory even while the product continues to ship.

What changed after 2023 is narrow. A capable AI coding assistant with access to a repository can produce a plausible, working implementation of a conventional requirement without being told the requirement. The build-instruction function — one of five — became partly free. Nothing happened to the other four. Most of the confusion in the field comes from teams observing that one-fifth of a document became unnecessary and concluding that the document did.

Five positions are now genuinely held by competent people. Each is stated below with the proposition its holders would sign and the one they would refuse, which is the only honest way to distinguish schools that agree on most sentences.

3. Mechanics in depth, with the arithmetic

The operational core is a per-sentence test, applied before writing rather than after. It has three movements, and expert practitioners run all three where amateurs run only the first.

The deletion test. If this sentence were absent, would a competent builder — with our repository, our design system and ordinary professional knowledge — produce something different? If no, the sentence describes a default and costs more to maintain than it saves.

The default-elicitation test. Say out loud what the default would be, before writing. This is the step usually left implicit, and it inverts the work: instead of describing the system you want, you describe the delta between the default and the system you want. Where the default is right, write nothing. Where the default is subtly wrong — a credit note issued in the ordinary way that is invalid under Indian GST timing rules; a pre-authorisation packet assembled sensibly but missing the treating doctor's registration number — that sentence is the most valuable in the document and deserves contractual care.

The two-reading test. Gause and Weinberg's discipline, now with higher stakes. Can a competent, unsympathetic reader implement this differently and still claim compliance? Under human execution, ambiguity surfaced as a question in a chat thread. Under literal execution it is resolved silently, fluently and invisibly, and arrives as finished work that looks correct.

Underneath these tests sits a quantity that can actually be estimated. Write the requirement if

p × r × C > w + (m × T)

where p is the probability that the builder's default differs from what you need; r is the probability that review fails to catch the difference; C is the cost if the difference reaches production; w is the cost of writing the sentence; m is the cost per period of maintaining it — keeping it true, re-reading it, and the risk that it goes stale and is executed anyway; and T is the number of periods the document is live.

The interesting term is r, because it is the one nobody measures and the one that varies most. Devika's team measured it directly over eleven features between December and February by seeding known deviations into generated candidates and observing whether review caught them. For conventional interface behaviour, review caught 96 per cent: r = 0.04. For domain rules — insurer-specific field requirements, timing windows, DPDP consent scope — review caught 72 per cent: r = 0.28. The reason is unsurprising once stated. A reviewer looking at a screen can see that a button is wrong. A reviewer looking at a screen cannot see that a rule is missing, because absence has no pixels.

Work one requirement through. Nirupan's rule: a pre-authorisation packet for a surgical admission must carry the treating doctor's registration number in a specific field, or the third-party administrator returns it unactioned. Estimate p = 0.9 — no general-purpose builder knows this. r = 0.28. C: Nirupan's hospitals submit about 4,200 such packets a month; at Nirupan's measured rework cost of ₹340 per returned packet, and an estimated three weeks before someone traced the pattern, C ≈ 2,900 × ₹340 ≈ ₹9.9 lakh, before the relationship cost. Expected cost of omission: 0.9 × 0.28 × ₹9.9 lakh ≈ ₹2.5 lakh. Cost of writing: six minutes of a PM's time, perhaps ₹90, plus maintenance. The sentence is worth roughly 2,700 times what it costs. Write it, and write it in the standing context so it never has to be written again.

Now the opposite. "The date picker should default to today." p = 0.2, r = 0.04, C perhaps ₹6,000 in a support ticket and a patch. Expected cost of omission: 0.2 × 0.04 × ₹6,000 = ₹48. Cost to write and maintain across eight quarters: ₹90 plus, say, ₹30 a quarter of re-reading and staleness risk — ₹330. Do not write it. Most PRDs written in 2022 consisted overwhelmingly of sentences of this second kind, which is why the practice felt wasteful long before anyone could prove it.

And a genuinely marginal one, to show the method has teeth rather than only confirming intuitions. "Station list paginates at fifty, not twenty-five." At Utsarg: p = 0.5, r = 0.1, C ≈ ₹40,000 (a measurable drop in reservation conversion for riders in dense Pune neighbourhoods, caught in a week). Expected cost of omission ₹2,000 against a write-and-maintain cost of ₹400. Write it — but the better move, which is what an expert does here, is to notice that this is a recurring judgement about list density and put it in the design system, converting a per-feature sentence into a standing one.

The second-order effect that dominates everything else

Thinning specifications does not remove work; it moves work from writing to reviewing. That would be a wash if review capacity scaled with build capacity. It does not, and the consequence is a queueing problem that Rohan's data was describing.

Treat the review stage as a single server. Before October, Squad Tarai produced about six reviewable changes a week and the squad's senior engineers could review about eight: utilisation ρ = 0.75. Using the standard M/M/1 approximation, expected time in queue is ρ ⁄ (μ(1−ρ)) = 0.75 ⁄ (8 × 0.25) = 0.375 weeks, about 1.9 days — which matches the observed 1.6. After adopting prototype-first, production rose to roughly fifteen candidates a week while review capacity stayed at eight. Utilisation above one is not a slower queue; it is an unbounded one, and the squad absorbed it by reviewing less carefully and by letting work sit. When Rohan's team throttled intake to about 7.6 a week to stabilise, ρ = 0.95 and expected queue time became 0.95 ⁄ (8 × 0.05) = 2.375 weeks — a little under twelve days, against the 9.4 observed.

The arithmetic is worth stating plainly because it is so counter-intuitive: raising the arrival rate from 6 to 7.6 per week — a 27 per cent increase in work admitted — multiplied waiting time by 6.3. The squad's "2.6× productivity" was almost entirely inventory.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as claims that could be false, then apply each to both companies.

Claim 1: the inferable share of a specification rises with the conventionality of the domain. Testable by reproduction rate — generate a candidate from intent alone and count how many of the original requirements it satisfies unprompted. At Utsarg, 38 of 44 (86 per cent). At Nirupan, 24 of 51 (47 per cent). The claim holds, and the spread is larger than most teams expect before they measure it.

Claim 2: inferability is a property of supplied context, not of the requirement. Both companies wrote standing-context documents and re-ran the test. Utsarg went from 86 to 93 per cent; Nirupan from 47 to 76. Nirupan gained far more, which inverts the usual intuition that regulated enterprises benefit least from this shift. They benefit most, because they have more durable, writable, reusable knowledge to bank.

Claim 3: thinning pays only where review capacity is slack. At Utsarg, false at the time of the decision: review was the binding constraint. At Nirupan, partly true — its bottleneck was customer-side user acceptance testing by hospital billing teams, which no change in specification practice would relieve.

Claim 4: where the cost of a silent wrong default is asymmetric, thinning is actively misleading. This is the condition under which the whole idea should be refused. Money movement, statutory timing windows, consent scope, clinical safety, anything with a regulator: the distribution of outcomes has a long left tail, and expected-value reasoning that uses an average cost understates it badly. At Nirupan, the rule is that any requirement touching a statutory obligation goes into Tier 1 and Tier 3 regardless of its reproduction rate, because the company must be able to demonstrate the requirement existed, not merely that the software behaves correctly.

That last point deserves emphasis because it is where residualist logic breaks. A residualist deletes a requirement the builder would satisfy anyway. An auditor does not ask whether the software is correct; the auditor asks to see the requirement, the approval and the test. Under that regime, inferability is irrelevant to whether you write it down — only to how much effort the writing takes.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product and platform. When a shared platform team serves four product teams, Tier 1 fragments. Whose standing context governs a payments module used by three products with different latency budgets? The honest answer, visible at Nirupan, is that standing context needs scoping rules exactly as code needs namespaces: a global tier, a product tier, and an explicit override protocol. Teams that skip this discover that their context file has contradictory statements and that the builder resolves the contradiction by picking one, silently.

Two-sided markets. The side you are not building for is invisible in every artefact the new practice produces. A prototype shows the buyer's screen. A generated candidate satisfies the buyer's intent. Neither says anything about what happens to seller incentives. Bhoomija Agri Networks, a Nashik company matching farmer producer organisations with institutional buyers, learned this in January: a generated candidate added a "lowest price first" default to the buyer's search, which no requirement had asked for and which would have restructured the market on the supply side. It was caught, but by a commercial manager who happened to look, not by any part of the process.

Regulated products. Traceability is a requirement about the document, not about the software, and no amount of builder capability touches it. Practically, the mature approach is to make Tier 3 the traceability spine — each statutory obligation gets an identifier, a test, and a link — and to let Tier 2 be genuinely thin. The compliance burden falls on structure rather than volume, which is a real gain; auditors prefer sixty linked, tested obligations to a four-hundred-page document nobody can navigate.

Hardware plus software. Utsarg's swap stations contain a physical dock with a tooling lead time of fourteen weeks. Software specifications can now be regenerated in a day; the moulded latch cannot. The seam between them is where the old discipline must survive intact, because a hardware specification error is not recoverable by regeneration. The practical rule mature hardware-plus-software companies use is that any requirement crossing the physical boundary reverts to the old standard of rigour, with the old change-control process, and the thin practice applies only above that line.

AI-native features. Here the notion of a requirement changes shape. "The assistant should correctly classify the rider's complaint" is not a requirement in the classical sense because behaviour is distributional. The specification becomes an eval set, a metric and a threshold, plus a stated policy for the tail. This is the clearest case where the formalists are simply right: the acceptance evidence is the specification, and prose about it is commentary.

The organisational seam. The most under-appreciated edge case. Thinning specifications inside a squad, where everyone shares context, is nearly free. Thinning at the boundary between functions — where the support lead, the compliance officer and the enterprise sales head used to learn what was coming by reading the PRD — removes an information channel that nothing has replaced. What mature companies actually do, as opposed to what they say, is keep a separate, short, outward-facing document for exactly this purpose and stop pretending it is the same artefact as the build specification.

6. Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Non-goals have become the highest-value sentences per word

The tell-tale sign is scope growth with no requesting stakeholder. When building was costly, scope crept because someone asked. Now it creeps because the builder is capable and generous: asked for a reservation screen, it adds a history view, an export and a notification preference, each plausible, each carrying permanent support surface. The obvious reading — "we should be stricter with stakeholders" — is wrong, because no stakeholder was involved.

Ambiguity and underspecification have separated

Underspecification is silence; a builder picks a reasonable default and usually that is fine. Ambiguity is a sentence with two competent readings. The expert's tell is a review conversation in which someone says "oh, I read that the other way" about work that is already complete. Under human execution ambiguity surfaced as a question before work started; now it surfaces as rework after work finishes, which is roughly twenty times more expensive.

Inferability is a property of context, so the context file is the real asset

The expert's tell is a team arguing about whether to write something down. The argument is malformed: the question is not whether to write it but at which tier. A practitioner who has internalised this stops writing domain rules into feature documents entirely, because a rule in a feature document is a rule that will be rewritten, slightly differently, next quarter.

Review misses absences, and domain rules are absences

The measured gap between r = 0.04 for visible interface deviations and r = 0.28 for missing domain rules is the single most useful empirical fact in this topic. The tell is a team that reviews by clicking through a build. Clicking finds what is wrong on screen; it cannot find what is not there. Expert review works from a pre-registered checklist derived from Tier 1, not from the artefact.

Writing was thinking, and the thinking has to be relocated on purpose

Naur's objection in operational form. The tell is a team whose documents read beautifully and whose edge-case defects rise — "fluent under-specification". The obvious reading is that they need better writers; the right reading is that enumerating the empty states was how they used to discover that a new hospital with zero submitted packets sees a screen implying an error. If you stop enumerating, you must add a deliberate discovery step, usually a structured adversarial pass over the generated candidate.

Stale text has changed from untidy to dangerous

Every long-lived document contains sentences nobody has read in two years. Under human execution they were inert. Under literal execution they are instructions, and they are executed faithfully. The tell is a team that has never deleted a requirement. The practical consequence is that specifications need code's hygiene — an owner, a date, a review cadence, and deletion treated as routine rather than as an admission of error.

A prototype cannot express a negative

This is the precise limit of the demonstrationist position and the sentence that ends most arguments about it. A prototype demonstrates one path through the system. It is silent about the paths it does not contain, about what must remain true when the system changes, and about anything the team decided not to do. The tell is a team that cannot answer "what must not break when we change this?" six weeks after shipping.

Acceptance evidence written afterwards is not evidence

If the threshold is set after seeing the result, review becomes negotiation and the document becomes a rationalisation. The tell is acceptance criteria whose numbers are suspiciously close to what the build achieved. Pre-registration — the test, the data, the number, dated before the work — is what converts review from re-deciding into checking, and it is the only mechanism that keeps review cheap enough to survive the higher arrival rate.

Velocity measured before the constraint is not velocity

The tell is a throughput improvement that does not appear in customer-facing lead time. Experts instrument the constraint, not the activity; the first question on hearing "we ship three times faster" is "at which stage, and what happened to the queue behind it?" Rohan's 2.6× and his 31 per cent were both correctly measured. Only one of them was a business result.

7. How this varies by product type and stage

Across consumer products the conventional default is frequently the right answer, because convention is what users have been trained to expect. Reproduction rates sit in the eighties. What survives is intent, the metric, genuinely brand-specific taste constraints, and the experiment design. In B2B and enterprise, a large fraction of every requirement is domain rule and contractual commitment that exists nowhere in general knowledge, so reproduction rates start far lower — but the gain from Tier 1 investment is far higher, because the knowledge is durable and reusable rather than feature-specific.

Platforms and marketplaces differ from both in kind rather than degree: the load-bearing content concerns effects on parties who do not appear in the artefact at all. Hardware imposes an irreversibility that regeneration cannot fix, and the old rigour must survive at the physical seam. AI products convert requirements into evaluation sets and thresholds, which is less a change of degree than a change of medium.

Where the difference is not real, it is worth saying so plainly. The coordination function and the record function are identical across all of these. Every product type needs someone outside the squad to know what is coming, and every product type needs the next person to be able to find out why a rule exists. Nothing about the product type changes that, and teams that reason from "we are a consumer company, we don't need documents" are confusing the build-instruction function with the other four.

By stage: in a company of ten, writer, builder and decider are often one person, so the transmission function is near zero and a specification may honestly be a paragraph — with the bill arriving at employee number twenty, who re-derives everything. Between roughly thirty and two hundred people, the record function becomes the binding one and most companies notice too late. Above that, coordination dominates, and the honest observation is that the build-instruction function was never the bulk of the work, which is why large firms that expected specification effort to halve have generally been disappointed.

Throughput settled at about 55 per cent above the old baseline, which is a good outcome that nobody would have described as a triumph in November.

9. Failure modes, with early warnings and diagnostics

Constraint amnesia. The team deletes the non-functional section because "the model knows best practice". Early warning: features that demonstrate beautifully and fail on cost or latency in production. Diagnostic question: ask three squad members for the p95 latency budget, the per-request cost ceiling and the data retention rule. Three different answers means it is written nowhere the builder can read. Cost of catching late: a re-architecture, typically one quarter.

The velocity illusion. Throughput at the build stage rises; throughput at the customer does not. Early warning: a growing gap between "candidates produced" and "changes released". Diagnostic: measure lead time from candidate-ready to released, and utilisation at the review stage. Cost of catching late: a quarter of inventory, and, worse, a strategy built on a number that was never real.

Fluent under-specification. Documents read well and edge-case defects rise. Early warning: the proportion of defects classed as "we never considered that case" climbing above about a fifth. Diagnostic: for the last three features, ask what the team decided not to do and why. Silence is the finding. Cost of catching late: the Naur cost — two personnel cycles later, nobody can explain the system.

Stale execution. Requirements nobody has read are implemented faithfully. Early warning: a defect whose root cause is "the document said so and the document was wrong". Diagnostic: sample ten requirements at random and ask the owner when each was last verified true. Cost of catching late: at Bhoomija, ₹34 lakh and a fortnight of the peak season.

Seam failure. A launch blocked in its final week by support, legal or finance. Early warning: functions outside the squad asking what is coming, in chat, repeatedly. Diagnostic: ask who outside the squad read the last three documents and what they did as a result. Cost of catching late: a delayed launch and a permanent erosion of trust in the product organisation, which is the expensive part.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Three disagreements are real, in the sense that well-informed practitioners hold opposite views and no available evidence settles them.

Does the durable context asset persist, or does it evaporate as models improve? The residualist bets that Tier 1 compounds: every rule banked is a rule never rewritten. The opposing view, held by serious people, is that as capability rises and tools read source systems directly, most of Tier 1 becomes inferable and the investment depreciates like any other write-down. The residualist's evidence is Nirupan's jump from 47 to 76 per cent, which is real money. The sceptic's evidence is that in eighteen months the reproduction rate at Utsarg rose from the low seventies to 86 with no change in practice. What would have to be true for the residualist to be wrong: that the non-inferable residue is mostly general knowledge arriving slowly, rather than private facts about your contracts, your customers and your decisions. Most of Nirupan's residue is the latter, which is why the residualist looks stronger in enterprise and weaker in consumer.

Is the theory-building objection a transitional complaint or a permanent one? Steelmanned, the Naur position says: a team that no longer writes the reasoning no longer holds it, and in two years it will be maintaining a system it cannot explain, with tooling that can regenerate any part and judgement about none of it. The opposing steelman is that the theory was always mostly in the code and the conversations, that PRDs were a poor vessel for it, and that a team reading and reviewing generated candidates is building theory more directly than a team writing prose about hypothetical screens. Both positions predict the same near-term data. They diverge at about the two-year mark, on handover. Nobody has that evidence yet at scale, and anyone claiming to is extrapolating.

Should acceptance evidence be prose or code? The formalist says anything checkable belongs in a checkable medium and that English acceptance criteria are a category error. The counter-position, held by people who have run regulated programmes, is that tests encode the what and lose the why, and that an auditor, a new joiner or a court needs the why. What would have to be true for the formalist to be fully right: that intent can be reconstructed from tests. It cannot; a test suite is silent on what would have been acceptable and was rejected. The practical settlement — prose for intent, code for acceptance, links between them — is not a synthesis anyone finds intellectually satisfying, and it is what most good teams do anyway.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic writes shorter documents. Someone who has internalised it does something different: they ask, before writing anything, what the builder would do by default, and they can usually say. They know their own reproduction rate, roughly, by feature class, because they have measured it rather than assumed it. They can name the three things in their product that nobody outside the company could possibly infer, and those three things are in a file with an owner and a date. They watch review utilisation the way an operations manager watches a bottleneck, and they are suspicious of throughput numbers measured anywhere else. They treat non-goals as the most expensive sentences to omit rather than as a courtesy section. They delete requirements routinely and without ceremony. And when a defect escapes, their instinct is not to add a paragraph to the feature document but to ask which tier the missing fact belonged in, so that the class of error cannot recur.

The negative tell is equally clear. Someone who has merely studied this will argue about document length. Length is an output, not a decision.

12. What each decided, and three questions

Rohan did not generalise Squad Tarai's practice. He generalised half of it: prototype-first for conventional consumer flows, with a hard rule that any requirement touching payments, the physical dock, or fleet-operator contracts reverts to the full standard. He also did the unglamorous thing, which was to add two senior reviewers and to publish review utilisation weekly beside throughput. His reasoning was that the squad's method was sound and its measurement was not, and that relieving the constraint was worth more than any further gain in build speed.

Devika accepted the 70 per cent target and redefined what it applied to. What a PRD Becomes When the Reader Can Build

A product requirements document was never one document. It was five jobs stapled together, and only one of them — telling a builder how to build — has become cheap. The craft now is knowing which of the other four you were doing by accident, and writing those down on purpose.

1. Bengaluru, 14 January 2026

Anuja Deshpande had two versions of the same feature sitting in staging, and she could not decide which of them frightened her more.

Anuja was group product manager at Prastut Retail Cloud, a Bengaluru company that sold distributor management software — order capture, stock, credit, claims and returns — to about 1,900 FMCG distributors across fourteen states: the firm in Nashik that moved biscuits into 4,000 kirana stores, the Coimbatore house that carried personal-care brands. Prastut did roughly ₹48 crore in annual recurring revenue and employed 240 people, engineering split between Bengaluru and Pune. It lived and died by how fast it absorbed changes to GST e-invoicing, since every distributor invoice had to carry an IRN from the government's Invoice Registration Portal.

In November, Anuja had run an experiment. Two squads would build the same quarter's roadmap under different specification rules. Squad A wrote PRDs the way Prastut had always written them: an average of 4,200 words, twenty to thirty-five numbered requirements, screen-by-screen behaviour. Squad B wrote what the engineering lead in Pune, Faizan Qureshi, called a "thin spec" — usually under 900 words — and then had the AI coding assistant produce a working candidate within a day, which the squad reviewed and corrected. Both squads shipped. Squad B shipped 40 per cent more, by story points, and its rework ratio was worse by half again. Two of its defects had reached a customer in Surat during the busiest fortnight of the year.

The planning meeting was on 30 January. Anuja had to say what Prastut's specification standard would be for the coming year, and the honest version of her problem was that neither squad's document was right. Squad A's PRDs contained a great deal of text that the assistant would have produced correctly without being told. Squad B's PRDs were missing the four or five sentences that would have prevented both defects. Nobody in the company could yet tell those two categories apart while writing.

2. The idea

Start with a definition. A product requirements document, or PRD, is a written artefact stating what a team intends to build and why, in enough detail that other people can act on it. It emerged in hardware and packaged software in the 1980s and 1990s for a now half-forgotten reason: the people who decided and the people who implemented were separated by weeks and often by continents, and the cost of an implementer guessing wrong was a manufacturing run. The document was a buffer against expensive misunderstanding.

That document was always doing at least five separate jobs. It transmitted intent: the user problem, why now, what success would look like. It transmitted build instructions: the behaviour in enough detail to implement without guessing. It performed coordination: telling support, legal, sales and finance what was coming so they could prepare. It created a record: six months later, why is the rounding rule like this? And it set acceptance: the basis on which someone would say the thing was done.

The change of the last few years is narrow and consequential. When the reader can build — an engineer working with a competent AI coding assistant, or an agent with access to the codebase — the second job collapses in value for everything conventional. A capable builder with sight of your repository infers the field validations, the pagination, the empty states, the error copy, the retry logic and the shape of the data model, because conventions are precisely what a model trained on the world's software has learned. What it cannot infer is everything true only of you: your intent, your constraints, the things you decided not to do, the domain rules living in a regulator's circular or a customer's contract, and the evidence you will accept as proof that the work is right.

The sentence Anuja could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "Write down only what a competent builder could not have derived from our code, our design system and common practice — which means intent, constraints, non-goals and acceptance evidence — and delete the rest."

3. How it actually works

The mechanic that makes this tractable is a test on individual sentences, not on documents. Take each line of a PRD and ask: if I deleted this, would a competent builder, working with our codebase and our design system, produce something different? If the answer is no, the line is describing a default, and it costs more to maintain than it saves. If the answer is yes, the line is load-bearing, and it is the reason the document exists.

That test has a sharper second form, which practitioners usually leave implicit. Ask what the builder's default actually is, out loud, before you write. If the default is what you wanted, delete your sentence. If the default is subtly wrong — if a reasonable builder would implement credit notes in the ordinary way and the ordinary way is illegal under Indian GST rules after a certain date — then that sentence is the single most valuable line in the document, and it should be written with the care you would give a contract clause.

The steps, in the order experienced teams run them: state intent and the metric; state constraints as numbers with units — latency budgets, cost ceilings, data residency, retention, the exact fields a customer's ERP expects; state non-goals explicitly, because a builder with surplus capacity is generous and will build adjacent things helpfully; enumerate only the edge cases where the plausible default is wrong; state acceptance evidence — the test, the dataset, the threshold — written before the work exists. Then the step almost everyone omits: decide where each durable fact should live. A GST rule is not a property of this feature; it is a property of the company, and it belongs in a standing context document the builder reads every time, not in a PRD that will be archived in April.

4. A worked example, line by line

Take the feature Squad B shipped in December: GST-compliant credit notes, the document a distributor raises when goods come back or a claim is settled. Prastut's original PRD had thirty-one numbered requirements across 4,200 words. In the last week of December, Faizan gave the assistant only the thin spec — intent, three constraints, two non-goals — plus access to the repository, and asked it to produce a candidate. He and Anuja then diffed the candidate's behaviour against the thirty-one original requirements and counted how many were satisfied without ever having been stated.

Twenty-two of thirty-one, or 71 per cent, were reproduced from context alone. That is the number that makes people excited and then makes them careless. The interesting nine are the rest.

Now the arithmetic on effort. The original PRD took about eleven hours to write and three hours of review across four functions: fourteen hours of specification cost. The thin spec took three and a half hours to write; reviewing the generated candidate took four, because reviewing working software is slower than reading prose. Call it seven and a half. The saving is six and a half hours per feature, and at roughly eleven such features a quarter, 71 hours — about 1.8 person-weeks.

Against that, the failure. Of the seven load-bearing requirements not reproduced, review caught five. Two escaped: the rule that a credit note against a supply must be issued before 30 November following the end of that financial year, and the reverse-charge case. Both reached a distributor in Surat. Remediation cost two engineer-days, one support escalation, and a credit note re-issued manually for ₹4.7 lakh of returned stock. The two stale requirements were implemented in full, because a literal reader does not know a screen was retired; a Prastut engineer would have said "this screen doesn't exist any more" and stopped. Net, Squad B saved 71 hours and spent about 30 on rework. A thin margin, and Anuja was right to be unimpressed.

The second pass — change one input. In the first week of January, Faizan spent nine hours writing a standing document: every GST and e-invoicing rule Prastut depended on, with the circular each came from, plus the ERP field maps for the eleven largest distributors, plus Prastut's latency and cost budgets. He re-ran the credit note test against that context. Reproduction rose from 22 of 31 to 28 of 31. Five of the six statutory rules were now inferred, because they were no longer buried in a PRD but sitting in a file the builder read every time.

This is the finding that reorganises the whole practice. Whether a requirement is "inferable" is not a fact about the requirement. It is a fact about the requirement given the context you have supplied. Every hour spent on durable context makes every future PRD thinner; every hour spent restating durable facts inside a per-feature PRD is spent again next quarter.

5. The nuances a learner must acquire

Non-goals become the highest-value lines in the document

When building was expensive, scope crept because stakeholders asked for more. When building is cheap, it creeps because the builder is helpful. Asked for a credit note screen, a capable assistant will cheerfully add bulk upload, an export and a dashboard — all plausible, none wanted, each carrying support cost forever. A non-goal such as "no bulk upload in this release; we have not decided how it interacts with claims approval" now does more work per word than any other kind of sentence.

Ambiguity has stopped failing loudly

Distinguish two things that get called the same name. Underspecification is when you have said nothing about a matter; a human engineer asks you, an assistant picks a sensible default, and usually that is fine. Ambiguity is when your sentence has two competent readings and you meant one of them. A human reader who notices ambiguity pings you on Slack. A literal reader resolves it silently, fluently, and finishes. Ambiguity now converts directly into confident, complete, wrong work — which is more expensive to detect than incomplete work, because it looks done.

Writing the detail was how you discovered the edge cases

The old PRD was not only a transmission device; it was a thinking device. Enumerating the empty states was how a PM discovered that a distributor with zero claims sees a screen that implies an error. If you delete the enumeration, you must relocate the thinking somewhere deliberate — usually into a structured review of the generated candidate — or you get fluent under-specification: documents that read well and omit the thing that matters.

Acceptance evidence must be written before the work exists

"It should feel fast" was tolerable when a human implementer would come back and negotiate. It is useless to a literal reader and worse than useless in review, because review then becomes re-deciding rather than checking. Acceptance evidence means a stated test on stated data with a stated threshold: p95 under 400 ms on the ten largest distributors' data; 60 real credit notes, all 60 matching the statutory fields. Pre-registering it is what makes review cheap.

Stale text has become dangerous rather than untidy

Every long-lived PRD contains sentences nobody has read in two years. Under human execution they were inert; an engineer knew the screen was gone. Under literal execution they are instructions. This is the strongest practical argument for treating the PRD as code: an owner, a date on every constraint, and deletion as a routine act rather than an admission of error.

A prototype is evidence, not a specification

Because prototypes are now nearly free, teams are tempted to let the prototype replace the document. A prototype answers "what does this feel like" better than any prose ever did. It cannot express a non-goal, a constraint, or a rule about a case it does not contain — a prototype is silent about the reverse-charge scenario precisely because nobody clicked it. What the prototype replaces is the interface description. What it cannot replace is everything invisible.

The document still has to outlive the people

Prastut's median PM tenure was 2.4 years; its median customer contract ran five. The record function of the PRD — why is this rounding rule like this, which regulator required it, who approved the exception for the Surat distributor — has nothing to do with building and does not get cheaper. If anything it matters more, because more decisions are now made per quarter.

Know what this cannot tell you

The deletion test tells you whether a sentence changes what gets built. It is silent on whether what gets built is worth building. No amount of specification discipline substitutes for having chosen the right problem, and a team that gets very good at thin specs will produce the wrong thing faster than before.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the conventional default is often the right answer, because conventions are what users have been trained to expect. Consumer PRDs therefore shrink the most; what survives is intent, the metric, brand-specific taste constraints, and the experiment design that will settle whether it worked.

In B2B and enterprise the opposite holds. Much of an enterprise requirement is domain rule and contractual commitment existing nowhere in the world's training data: a GST circular, an insurer's cashless framework, a customer's SLA, one distributor's ERP field names. Those are not inferable at any level of model capability, because they are not general knowledge. Enterprise PRDs shrink least, and the standing-context asset is largest.

In marketplaces the critical content is the side of the market you are not currently thinking about. A change obviously good for buyers is exactly what a builder will implement well; the line that must be written is the one saying sellers' ranking must not change, and why. Incentive effects cannot be inferred from a repository at all.

By stage: in a ten-person company the writer, builder and decider are often the same person, so the transmission job is nearly zero and a PRD may honestly be a paragraph — the cost, paid eighteen months later, is that nothing survives. In a large company the coordination and record jobs always dominated, and the build-instruction job, the only one that got cheap, was never the bulk of the work. Firms that expected specification effort to halve are generally disappointed.

7. Common mistakes

Deleting the constraints because "the model knows best practice"

Symptom from the outside: features that demonstrate beautifully and fail in production on cost, latency or privacy. Underlying misunderstanding: treating constraints as engineering detail rather than as business decisions. Cheapest diagnostic: ask any three people on the squad for the p95 latency budget, the per-request cost ceiling and the data retention rule. If you get three answers, they are not written down anywhere the builder can read.

Thin spec, thick rework

Symptom: two exhilarating sprints followed by a growing review queue. Misunderstanding: that the work saved in writing was saved outright, rather than moved into review. Diagnostic: measure the proportion of merged work that was re-specified after someone saw it. At Prastut it was 9 per cent in Squad A and 23 per cent in Squad B.

Treating the generated prototype as the specification

Symptom: six weeks later nobody can answer "what must remain true if we change this?" Misunderstanding: confusing a demonstration of one path with a statement about all paths. Diagnostic: ask the team to name the three cases the prototype does not contain.

Writing for the builder and forgetting everyone else

Symptom: a launch blocked at the last week by support, legal or finance. Misunderstanding: that the PRD's only reader is now the builder. Diagnostic: ask who outside the squad read the last three documents, and what they did as a result.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Anuja's decision looks unglamorous. The team maintains one standing context document, owned by a named engineer, dated, containing the conventions, the statutory rules with their sources, and the numeric budgets. Per-feature documents run 600 to 1,000 words and contain four things: intent with a metric, constraints that are numbers, non-goals, and acceptance evidence written before any code exists. Every feature begins with the question "what would a competent builder do here by default?", and the PRD says only where that default is wrong. The candidate implementation arrives in a day and the review is a checking exercise against pre-registered evidence, not a negotiation. When a case escapes review, the fix is added to the standing context, not to the feature document — so the same class of error cannot recur.

9. What Anuja decided

On 30 January, Anuja did not choose between Squad A and Squad B. She proposed that Prastut split its specification into two tiers: a standing context file, owned by Faizan, reviewed monthly, holding everything durable; and a per-feature brief capped at 1,000 words holding intent, constraints, non-goals and acceptance evidence. The budget she asked for was not engineering time but two weeks of a senior PM's time to write the standing document properly, on the argument that nine hours had already moved six requirements from "must be stated" to "inferred", and there were a great many more where those came from.

Her reasoning was that Squad B's real error was not thinness. It was thinness without a place to put the durable facts, so they simply vanished. What to learn next follows directly: reviewing work you did not write, because the hours saved in writing reappear in review, and review is now the scarce skill rather than specification.

Two questions to sit with.

1. Take the last document you wrote. Which sentences would change what gets built if you deleted them — and of the rest, how many did you write because they were needed, and how many because their absence would have looked unprofessional?

2. If "inferable" depends on the context you supply, who in your organisation owns that context, and when was it last wrong?

Nyasa Technologies: What Is Left to Write

1. Pune, Sunday 20 September 2026, 11.40 p.m.

Nandita Rege had three documents open and no way to reconcile them.

On the left of her screen was the engineering pre-read for Wednesday's board meeting, which said that Nyasa Technologies had reduced its median cycle time by 58 per cent in nine months. In the middle was a message from Lavanya Pillai in Singapore, sent at 6.12 p.m. Dubai time, forwarding a note from Mizaan Financial Services: the specification package due under clause 9.3 of their agreement had to be delivered by 30 September, and Mizaan's compliance head would like to schedule a walkthrough. On the right was the incident report from July, forty-one pages, which Nandita had now read four times and which still did not answer the only question she cared about — whether the ₹1.9 crore of mis-stated interest at Sarvottam Finance had been caused by the way Nyasa now wrote its specifications, or by something else entirely that the new way of working had merely made easier to see.

Her chief technology officer wanted a decision on Monday morning. The board met on Wednesday the 24th. The monsoon had finally broken over Baner and the window was open, and Nandita was aware that she had been reading the same paragraph of the incident report for twenty minutes.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2023

Nyasa Technologies was founded in Pune in 2018 to sell lending operations software — origination, underwriting workflow, disbursal, servicing, collections — to India's non-banking financial companies and urban co-operative banks. By September 2026 it served 61 lenders, ran ₹68 crore of annual recurring revenue, and employed 340 people. Its engineering was split between Pune and Bengaluru; its implementation consultants, who configured the product for each lender, sat mostly in Pune and Coimbatore.

The decision that shaped everything since was taken in March 2023, to win Sarvottam Finance. Sarvottam was a Pune-headquartered NBFC with a ₹4,100 crore book across two-wheeler, gold and small-business lending, and it had been burned by a previous vendor whose customisations could not be audited. Sarvottam's condition was absolute: every lending rule — eligibility, pricing, penal charges, foreclosure, co-lending splits — had to live in a versioned, exportable rule book that its own compliance team could read, diff and place in front of an RBI inspector. Not in code. Not in a developer's head.

Nyasa built it. The Rulebook architecture, as it came to be called internally, was the reason the company won Sarvottam — ₹9.4 crore of annual recurring revenue, its largest account — and then eleven more lenders on the same argument. It was also the reason for a consequence nobody weighed at the time. Because the domain logic lived in configuration rather than in code, the codebase itself contained remarkably little knowledge about lending. A reader of the repository could learn how Nyasa's rule engine evaluated a rule. It could learn almost nothing about what an Indian NBFC is required to do when a borrower part-prepays a loan.

3. The industry around it

The market Nyasa sold into was defined more by regulation than by competition. The RBI's digital lending guidelines set out what a lending service provider may and may not do; the Account Aggregator framework, operating under Sahamati, governed how consented financial data moved; CKYC governed identity; the DPDP Act of 2023 governed everything else about personal data, with its consent and purpose-limitation obligations still settling into practice. Co-lending arrangements between banks and NBFCs, which had grown quickly, carried their own settlement and reporting rules, and it was in the co-lending module that Nyasa's July incident had occurred.

Competitively, Nyasa sat among capable Indian firms — Lentra, FinBox, Perfios and Yubi in adjacent parts of the stack — in a market where Indian software companies had global credibility that Freshworks, Zoho and Postman had helped establish. Lenders increasingly expected UPI-grade reliability and Zerodha-grade interfaces from back-office software, which was not a comparison that flattered anyone in the sector.

Nyasa's exposure outside India was new and concentrated. In January 2026 it had signed Mizaan Financial Services, a Dubai lender operating across the UAE and Oman, for ₹4.1 crore a year. The Mizaan contract had been written by lawyers in a jurisdiction where documentation obligations are taken literally, and clause 9.3 required a specification package — functional specification, data-flow description, and a traceability matrix linking each regulatory obligation to a test — for each release. Rohit Khanna, Nyasa's sales head in New Jersey, had two American prospects waiting on a similar module for US state-level lending rules.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In December 2025, Vikram Salunke, Nyasa's chief technology officer, ran a two-squad trial of AI-assisted development. The results were unambiguous enough that in January he proposed extending it to all nine squads, together with a change to how work was specified: the seven-section requirements template, which averaged 4,800 words per feature, would be replaced by a one-page brief.

The belief at the time, stated plainly in the January proposal, was that "the majority of our requirements documents restate what the system already does, and the assistant reads the system directly." Nandita had agreed. She had written in the margin of the proposal: agree for workflow and interface; what about the Rulebook? The question was discussed for eleven minutes in a meeting on 14 January and deferred.

Through February and March, throughput rose. In April the engineering team re-baselined its story-point scale, on the reasonable grounds that the old scale had been calibrated against a slower process. In May, customer support changed its ticket taxonomy, moving a category previously called "configuration error — customer" into "product defect" after Sarvottam objected that the old label attributed Nyasa's mistakes to its own staff.

On 11 July, a Saturday, Sarvottam's operations head called. On loans where a borrower had made a part-prepayment and subsequently rescheduled, interest was being recalculated on the original principal for one cycle before correcting itself. The convention implemented was the one used in several international markets and was, in the abstract, defensible. It was not what Sarvottam's rule book said, and it was not what the RBI's fair practices expectations would support. Two thousand eight hundred and forty loans were affected; ₹1.9 crore of interest was mis-stated; Sarvottam refunded ₹1.42 crore and reported the matter to its own board.

The incident report, delivered on 6 August, found that the behaviour had entered through a generated implementation of a servicing change, reviewed and merged on 3 June, in which the part-prepayment interaction had not been specified because — the report's words — "the requirement was considered inferable from existing behaviour." What the report also found, in an appendix that received much less attention, was that the corresponding rule in Sarvottam's rule book had been edited on 22 May by an implementation consultant in Coimbatore, in a way that was individually correct and interacted badly with the June code change. The report did not say which of the two was the cause. It said both were necessary.

5. The people

Nandita Rege, chief product officer, Pune. Five years at Nyasa. Position: the company thinned its specifications without deciding where the durable knowledge would live, and is now discovering that it does not know where it lives. Incentive: she signed the January proposal. Not saying: she has begun to suspect that the specification question is a proxy for something she has avoided for two years, which is that Nyasa has never decided whether the Rulebook is a product feature or the company's actual specification.

Vikram Salunke, chief technology officer, Pune. Position: the July incident was a review failure and a configuration-governance failure, not a specification failure; reverting the practice would cost the company its only real efficiency gain. Incentive: his engineering efficiency target is written into the Series C narrative. Not saying: he has already shown the 58 per cent figure to two prospective investors.

Meera Chandrasekhar, head of compliance, Mumbai. Position: Nyasa cannot demonstrate traceability from regulatory obligation to requirement to test, and an RBI inspection of Sarvottam in the coming quarter will reach Nyasa as a service provider. Position: the codebase has never contained the domain knowledge and never will, because of the 2023 architecture, so the thin-spec argument was imported from companies whose situation is the opposite of Nyasa's. Incentive: professional pride in the Rulebook, which he built. Not saying: since May he has been writing, on weekends, a 14,000-word document of lending rules and their regulatory sources, and has not told anyone because he expects to be told it duplicates the rule book.

Incentive: he built the dashboard and does not want it discredited. Not saying: he wrote both caveats in a comment on the dashboard definition page in April, where nobody read them, and has not raised them in a meeting.

8. The options as Nandita sees them

Option one — reinstate the full standard for anything touching money or regulation. Workflow and interface work continues under the thin practice; the co-lending, servicing, penal-charge and consent modules revert to the seven-section template with traceability. The evident cost is that these four modules are roughly 55 per cent of the roadmap and the reversion would consume most of the efficiency gain. Vikram will argue, with Exhibit 4 in hand, that the gain was worth only ₹31 lakh gross anyway; Meera will argue that the Sarvottam exclusion makes that number meaningless.

Option two — keep the thin practice and build the acceptance layer. Instead of prose, invest in an executable compliance suite: every obligation becomes a test with an identifier, and the test suite becomes the traceability artefact for both the RBI and Mizaan. The attraction is that it addresses Exhibit 5 directly and is compatible with the speed. The cost is that Nyasa has 23 such tests and needs at least 47, the work is specialised, and the two people who could write them are Ashwin and one engineer in Pune, both fully committed until November.

Option three — make the Rulebook the specification. Take Ashwin's weekend document, fund it properly, and declare that the versioned rule book plus a written layer of regulatory sources is the company's requirements artefact — read by the implementation consultants, read by the assistant, exportable to a customer's compliance team. The attraction is that it uses the 2023 architecture rather than fighting it. The cost is that it makes a customer-facing configuration artefact into an internal engineering dependency, and nobody has thought through what happens when a consultant in Coimbatore edits it on a Friday evening.

Nandita had written all three on a sheet of paper and had then written, underneath, a sentence she had not shown anyone: all three assume the problem is the document. The July incident required a configuration change and a code change, three weeks apart, in two cities, and there is no specification standard that would have connected them — because the configuration edit is not part of any release process at all. And there is the other thing, which is that Nyasa has perhaps three people who can review a lending rule with authority, all of them in the same two-hour window of the working day, and every option on the sheet increases what they have to look at.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets on Wednesday 24 September and Vikram's slide is already in the pack. Mizaan's clause 9.3 package is contractually due on 30 September; the contract is ₹4.1 crore a year and carries a termination-for-breach clause with a thirty-day cure period. An RBI inspection of Sarvottam is expected during the October–December quarter and will, as a matter of routine, reach Nyasa as a service provider. Hiring is frozen until the Series C closes, which Vikram's efficiency narrative is part of; the two open positions in Pune have been open since June. Ashwin has ten days of leave booked from 4 October for a family wedding in Kochi, deferred twice already. And Diwali falls on 8 November, after which Nyasa's implementation teams historically lose about three weeks to customer-side holidays.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What do Exhibits 1 and 2 actually establish, and what would you need in order to compare either series across the April and May changes?

2. Exhibit 3 shows reproduction rates of 86 per cent for two features and 16 to 22 per cent for three others. What explains the spread, and what does that imply about which requirements Nyasa should still be writing down?

3. Exhibit 4 excludes the Sarvottam refund on the grounds that the root cause is contested. Is that the right treatment? Construct the version of the exhibit you would take to the board, and state your assumptions.

4. Exhibit 5 measures a gap that exists even where the software is correct. Which function of a requirements document does it measure, and can any of the three options close it by 30 September?

5. Nandita's private note says all three options assume the problem is the document. If she is right, what is the problem — and what evidence in the case supports your answer over hers?

6. What should Nandita do on Monday morning, in her first three meetings, and what should she say to the board on Wednesday about a 58 per cent improvement that her own chief technology officer has already shown to investors?

11. Baner, 1.10 a.m.

Nandita had by now closed the incident report and opened, instead, the file Ashwin had sent her at ten that evening with a one-line message: "This is what I've been doing on weekends. It is not finished and it is probably the wrong shape. But somebody had to write it down." Fourteen thousand words of lending rules, each with its regulatory source, each dated, several marked with a query where Ashwin himself was unsure. It was, she thought, the most useful document anyone at Nyasa had produced in two years, and it had been written in secret by an engineer who expected to be told it was a duplicate.

She thought about Meera's sixteen obligations, and about the fact that Meera's own register said twenty-one and neither of them could say which number was right. She thought about Lavanya's question, which was really a question about whether Nyasa would rather be late or be wrong, and about the fact that she had not answered it. She thought about Anselm reviewing three plausible candidates at nine at night in Berlin, and wondered how long he would keep doing that.

Somewhere in the building the generator had cut in. Nandita made a note of the three things she would say on Monday, read it, and deleted the second one. Then she sat looking at the remaining two, which did not, on their own, make an argument.

Nibandh Systems: The Specification Standard Before Diwali

1. Bengaluru, Thursday 10 September 2026

The quarterly planning lock was eight days away, and Shalini Iyer had been asked a question she could not answer with the evidence in front of her.

Shalini was director of product at Nibandh Systems, on the fourth floor of an office block off Old Airport Road in Bengaluru. That morning her VP of engineering, Karthik Narayanan, joining from Pune, had put a single slide on the screen: Proposal — retire the PRD template, effective Q3. Below it were three lines from the August pilot. Two features built without a requirements document had reached staging in three days each, against nine days for the one built the old way. Karthik's argument was that the engineers now had AI coding assistants with access to the whole repository, that they were producing working candidates faster than anyone could write documents about them, and that Nibandh was paying its product managers to describe things the assistants already knew.

Shalini had the other half of the same pilot in her notes. One of those two fast features had put a defect into production at a large personal-care customer during the last week of August, and the company had spent ₹6.4 lakh cleaning it up.

By Thursday 18 September the quarter's plan would be locked. Nibandh had committed to two things in that quarter that it could not miss: the festive returns wave, which peaks in the fortnight after Diwali on 8 November, and the go-live of its first Gulf customer on 15 November. Shalini had to say what the specification standard would be before either.

2. Nibandh Systems

Nibandh was founded in 2019 by two engineers who had left a Chennai enterprise-software company, on a straightforward observation: Indian e-commerce had solved forward logistics well and reverse logistics badly. A brand selling on its own website, on Flipkart, on Meesho and on Nykaa faced four different return windows, four different quality-check protocols, four different settlement cycles, and one very unhappy customer-service team reconciling them in spreadsheets.

Nibandh sold the software that sat in the middle. It ingested return requests from every channel a brand sold on, applied the brand's own eligibility rules, booked a reverse pickup with Delhivery, Shadowfax or Ekart, tracked the quality check at the warehouse, issued the GST credit note, and pushed the refund through Razorpay. By September 2026 it served about 420 direct-to-consumer brands, ran ₹34 crore of annual recurring revenue, and employed 165 people. In an ordinary month it processed roughly 4.2 lakh return requests; in the fortnight after Diwali the previous year it had processed 11 lakh in fourteen days.

Its competitors were real and capable: Unicommerce and Vinculum at the enterprise end, ClickPost in logistics intelligence, and — always — the possibility that a large brand would decide to build it in-house. Nibandh's engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune. Its design lead, Hanna Brandt, worked from Berlin. Its data scientist, Aditi Rao, was in Toronto. Its customer-success lead for international accounts, Priya Menon, was in Singapore, and its sales head, Rakesh Grover, worked out of New Jersey, chasing the Indian-origin D2C brands selling into North America.

In July 2026 Nibandh had signed Aqeeq Trading Group, a Dubai retail house running four fashion and home brands across the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The contract was worth about ₹2.8 crore a year — Nibandh's largest single account by a wide margin, and its first outside India. It committed Nibandh to a GCC-ready release by 15 November: UAE VAT tax credit notes rather than GST credit notes, an Arabic right-to-left interface, and returns eligibility under UAE consumer-protection rules rather than marketplace-specific Indian windows.

3. The situation

Karthik's pilot had run through August across three features. Exhibit 1 shows what happened.

The expensive defect had a specific cause. The bulk return approval feature generated GST credit notes that did not carry a reference to the original invoice's IRN — the identifier issued by the government's Invoice Registration Portal. The implementation was reasonable, conventional and wrong, and nobody reviewing the screen could see the omission, because a missing field reference is not visible in an interface.

Shalini had then done something Karthik had not. She took the bulk return approval feature's original, unused PRD from the backlog — thirty-eight numbered requirements — and checked, one by one, how many of them the assistant had satisfied without ever being told. Exhibit 2 is the result.

The team saw this from four places and four points of view. In Pune it looked like proof that the documents were mostly waste. In Berlin, Hanna saw a design system being quietly rewritten feature by feature, since a builder given no guidance invents its own spacing and its own empty states. In Singapore, Priya saw the Aqeeq go-live and asked a question nobody could answer: which document would she hand Aqeeq's compliance officer to show that UAE VAT treatment had been specified rather than guessed? And from New Jersey, Rakesh wanted to know when the same release would support US return rules, because he had two brands waiting.

4. The people

Shalini Iyer, director of product, Bengaluru. Eight years at Nibandh's scale of company, three of them here. She has to hold both the Diwali wave and the Aqeeq commitment, and she is aware that if she simply refuses Karthik's proposal she will be the person who slowed engineering down in the quarter it finally got fast.

Karthik Narayanan, VP engineering, Pune. He has an engineering objective for the year that is stated in cycle time, and the pilot moved it more than anything in three years. He believes, sincerely, that the two escaped defects were review failures rather than specification failures, and that better review is cheaper than more documents. He is also carrying two unfilled roles and a team that is tired.

Hanna Brandt, design lead, Berlin. Her working day overlaps Bengaluru by about three hours in the evening. She wants the interface decisions to stop being made inside generated candidates she sees only at review, and she is the only person who has read the Arabic right-to-left requirements carefully. Her ask is specific and modest: write down what a feature is not going to do, because she can no longer tell from the build.

Priya Menon, customer-success lead for international accounts, Singapore. She owns the Aqeeq relationship and travels to Dubai monthly. Aqeeq's compliance officer has asked for documentation showing how VAT credit notes are produced and where customer data is stored — a routine request in the GCC, and one Priya currently cannot satisfy from a paragraph and a prototype.

5. The options

Option A — Keep the existing PRD template for everything. Nothing changes; the pilot is treated as an experiment that failed. The upside is that the Aqeeq documentation exists by default and the GST class of defect is unlikely to recur. The cost is arithmetic: at twelve PM hours and nine build days per feature, the GCC release and the festive hardening cannot both clear the 8 October freeze without cutting roughly a third of the scope, and Karthik's team will read it as a vote of no confidence in the month it finally shipped fast.

Option B — Retire the PRD, as Karthik proposes. Product managers write a paragraph of intent; engineers generate candidates; the team reviews the working software. The upside is real and measured: three days instead of nine, and a happier engineering organisation. The cost is that the eleven requirements in Exhibit 2 that no builder could infer have nowhere to live, and the GCC release consists almost entirely of that kind of requirement — VAT treatment, Arabic layout, UAE eligibility rules, data residency — for a customer who will ask to see them written down.

Option C — Split the specification in two. Build one standing document, owned by engineering, holding everything durable: the GST and VAT rules with their sources, the marketplace return windows, the customer-specific configurations, the design system's rules, and Nibandh's latency and data-residency commitments. Then cap the per-feature brief at roughly 800 words containing only four things — intent and the metric, constraints as numbers, explicit non-goals, and the acceptance tests written before any code exists. The upside is that the eleven non-inferable requirements are captured once rather than per feature, and Priya gets a document to hand Aqeeq. The cost is about eight working days of senior time in the next two weeks, taken out of a quarter that has none to spare, and it will not be complete before the GCC work starts.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 shows the thin-spec features were three times faster to build and produced three escaped defects. Is that a specification problem or a review problem? What in Exhibit 2 helps you decide?

2. Of the fourteen requirements not reproduced in Exhibit 2, which would still not be reproduced if Nibandh wrote nothing further, and which would become inferable if the right context existed somewhere the builder could read?

3. Priya's request from Aqeeq is for documentation, not for correct software. Which of the PRD's jobs is that, and does any amount of builder capability reduce it?

4. What should Shalini take to the planning lock on 18 September, and what does she give up to pay for it?

7. A note for the learner

The lens that makes this case tractable is the question of what a requirements document is for once the reader can build. A PRD was never one thing. It transmitted intent, it gave build instructions, it coordinated other functions, it created a record, and it fixed acceptance. Only the second of those five became cheap when the assistant arrived. Karthik's proposal treats the collapse of one job as the collapse of the document; Option A treats the survival of four jobs as a reason to change nothing.

Exhibit 2 is the evidence that separates the two. Sixty-three per cent of the requirements were reproduced from context alone, which vindicates Karthik's instinct that most of what Nibandh wrote was waste. But the residue is not a random sample of the whole. It is exactly the material that is specific to Nibandh — a GST rule, a marketplace policy, a customer's warehouse codes — plus three stale lines that a human engineer would have questioned and a literal reader built without hesitation. A good answer notices that "inferable" is not a property of a requirement but of the context supplied to the builder: a GST rule is unknowable from the repository and entirely knowable from a file that states it.

One defensible path is Option C, with a sequencing decision attached. Shalini should take Option C to the planning lock, but not as a two-week project that blocks the release. She should scope the standing document to the two things this quarter actually requires — the tax rules for both India and the UAE, and the customer-specific configurations — and defer the rest to December. That is perhaps three days of work, not eight. She should adopt the 800-word brief immediately, with non-goals made mandatory because they cost nothing and answer Hanna's problem directly. And she should require pre-registered acceptance tests for anything touching money or tax, which is where both escaped defects came from and where the Aqeeq contract concentrates its risk.

The reasoning is that this concedes Karthik's finding rather than resisting it — the documents really were mostly waste, and speed is real — while refusing his conclusion, because the waste and the value were unevenly distributed and the pilot's two defects landed precisely on the valuable part. It also gives Priya something to hand Aqeeq's compliance officer, which neither A nor B does well: Option A produces four hundred pages nobody can navigate, and Option B produces nothing at all.

The test Shalini can teach her PMs in a sentence: before writing anything, say out loud what a capable builder would do here by default. Where the default is right, write nothing. Where the default is wrong, that sentence is the most valuable one in the document — and it probably belongs in the standing file, not in this brief.
